newsitem.title: USA: Multinationals plan to send more managers abroad.
newsitem.headline: Multinationals plan to send more managers abroad.

text.p: Global corporations plan a significant increase in the number of senior managers they will send abroad to gain experience, a scholarly survey reports.
Already, many transnationals have begun to "globalize" their executives, the better to prepare them "for future competitive success," the survey noted.

"Selecting future senior executives based on their international experience sends a key signal to employees that international perspectives and skills count," asserted the survey's authors, management professors Hal Gregersen of Brigham Young University in Provo, Utah, and J. Stewart Black of Thunderbird University in Glendale, Ariz.

Currently, they noted, only 36 percent of European, 14 percent of Japanese and none of the American companies surveyed "actually required international experience as a prerequisite for becoming a senior manager."

"In the future," Gregersen and Black predicted, "most firms in all three areas plan to expatriate managers more frequently." One-third of the global businesses surveyed plan no change in their expatriation policies and relatively few -- 12 percent to 25 percent -- plan to scale back this training approach, they said.

Experience abroad, the researchers said, increases executives' ability "to think globally and act locally. Executives must develop an understanding of the global marketplace, yet have the ability to implement at the local level."

The survey, completed last year, was designed to compare contemporary practices with future trends in global leader development, including expatriation, inpatriation, foreign travel, and task force project teams.

Gregersen and Black gathered data from international human resources directors at 139 large transnationals, having on average 50,000 employees. Of these, 69 companies were based in Europe and 35 each in Japan and the United States.
Currently, among their top managers, only 35 percent of those from Europe, 27 percent of those from Japan, and 15 percent of those from the U.S. have had international assignment experience.

By contrast, 49 percent of both European and Japanese human resources officials said their organisations plan to increase expatriation of executives, as did 43 percent of human resources officials at U.S. firms.

U.S. companies, the study found, have gone the furthest toward becoming "internationalized." Among their subsidiaries, 55 percent of top management jobs are filled by foreigners, compared with 47 percent for European and 23 percent for Japanese firms.

Inpatriation -- the process of bringing foreign nationals to work on assignment in the home country -- "is not used as extensively as expatriation to develop global leaders," Gregersen and Black reported.

In fact, 92 percent of Japanese transnationals said they plan to continue their "no inpatriation" policy and U.S. firms reported they were divided evenly between not changing and increasing inpatriation. Seven of 10 European companies, though, said they plan to import more foreign nationals.
Global corporations, the study learned, prefer to develop their managers by executive training rather than by recruiting internationalists.
Training methods employed include seminars, foreign travel, and the use of task force or project teams.

Whereas Japanese companies develop their leaders through extensive foreign travel and management training, their U.S. counterparts "placed a very high premium on task force and project teams," Gregersen and Black found.

"Many firms have initiated a globalization strategy for their managers," the study's authors conclude, "but a more systematic and extensive approach to international training and development is required for future competitive success."
(Sherwood Ross is a free-lance writer who covers workplace topics for Reuters.)
